name: Sara Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential and isn't linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Three mornings a week I'm the class pianist at the Kessler Ballet School, playing for the barre exercises, pliés, tendus, all of it, while Mrs Kessler counts and shouts. Then four evenings I play the piano in the lounge bar at the Hotel Meridian, from seven till eleven, old standards and soft pop for people having a drink after meetings. I read music well enough but I'm slow at improvising, so I stick to what I know. My boyfriend Ruben drives a city bus, so our hours rarely line up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about that week, and what's hard about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the routine, honestly. Same piano, same corner, same barman, Nico, who slides me a coffee at nine. The hard part is that nobody listens in the hotel, and in the ballet school I'm basically a human metronome. The hotel pays a fixed monthly fee on a two-year contract and I've got about four months saved, so it's steady, which is why I took it. I don't use any of these AI apps, I don't even like my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, there you go, people panicked over nothing. I'm not really one for posting, so I'd mostly say it to Nico and Ruben over dinner. Maybe I'd say I'm glad I didn't waste time learning it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays as it is, which I like. The hotel contract runs two more years and the ballet school's been around for thirty. Nothing in that card touches a piano in a hotel lounge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Exactly what I do now. Play the mornings, play the evenings, keep putting a bit into savings each month. Maybe learn a few newer songs because guests keep asking for things I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit bored by the question, if I'm honest. It's the world I already live in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in that steady life that does worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that the contract ends in two years and I'm not sure they'll renew. But hotels like a pianist; it's part of the furniture. The Hotel Meridian has had a pianist in the lounge since 1962, and nobody wants to be the manager who ends that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which newer songs do guests ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Film songs mostly, and whatever's been on the radio. I'd buy the sheet music and practise a couple a month at the ballet school before class. Mrs Kessler doesn't mind as long as I'm finished by nine.

say: I'd say people **panicked over nothing** and I'm glad I didn't learn it.
I'd mostly say it **in person** to Nico and Ruben, not online.
think: My **hotel contract** and the ballet school feel steady for the next two years.
Nothing in this picture touches a **piano in a lounge**.
do: Keep playing **mornings** at the ballet school and **evenings** at the hotel.
Learn a couple of **newer songs** guests ask for each month.
feel: **Calm** and a little **bored**, since it's the world she already lives in.
S0.quote: The Hotel Meridian has had a pianist in the lounge since 1962, and nobody wants to be the manager who ends that.
fieldNote: Her **fixed monthly fee** and two-year contract are why she feels secure.
She avoids technology and is quietly **proud of not learning** AI tools.
Her only worry is **contract renewal**, which she plays down.

steps.text: Keep playing ballet classes in the mornings and the hotel lounge at night
Buy sheet music for two new film songs each month
Put a fixed sum into savings after each monthly fee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there are things a machine shouldn't do, and playing for dancers is one of them. I'd say it to Mrs Kessler, who'd agree. But I wouldn't make a big fuss in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I've heard there are already apps that follow the teacher's count and play along. If the bigger ballet schools start using one, Mrs Kessler might feel she has to. That's about a third of my money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself more useful at the school, maybe offer to play for the exams and the summer show as well. I'd ask the hotel for a fifth evening if they'd have me. I wouldn't learn the apps myself, that's not what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not frightened, but I'd notice every time Mrs Kessler mentioned costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Mrs Kessler asked you to run the app instead of playing, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say no. I'm a pianist, not a button presser. I'd rather lose the mornings at the ballet school than sit next to a piano pressing play on a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: That's a third of your income. How would you cover it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hotel, if they gave me another evening, and savings for a while. Ruben's wage would cover more of the rent for a bit, which he wouldn't mind. I'd find a church or a school concert that needs an accompanist.

say: I'd say playing for **dancers** is something a machine shouldn't do.
I wouldn't make a **public fuss** about it.
think: Accompaniment **apps** could take the ballet mornings, a **third** of my income.
The **hotel lounge** still feels safe in this picture.
do: Offer to play the ballet school's **exams and summer show**.
Ask the hotel for a **fifth evening**.
Refuse to learn or run any **accompaniment app**.
feel: **Uneasy**, noticing every time Mrs Kessler mentions **costs**.
S1.quote: I'd rather lose the mornings at the ballet school than sit next to a piano pressing play on a machine.
fieldNote: She splits her job clearly: **ballet mornings** at risk, **hotel nights** safe.
Her refusal to run an app is about **pride** in being a pianist.
**Ruben's wage** is a quiet safety net she counts on.

steps.text: Offer to play the ballet school's exams and summer show

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to think about people before companies, and fast. I'm not political, but two years is mad. I'd say it to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the ballet mornings go first, because the music for class is the kind of thing a computer would do perfectly. The hotel is different, a robot pianist wouldn't come till 2031. But if the businesspeople stop travelling because their jobs are gone, the lounge is empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything extra and keep the four months. I'd try to get a second hotel or a restaurant that wants live piano. Maybe I'd teach beginners piano at home, children, because parents still want a person for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The hotel is my anchor and I can picture it getting quieter and quieter until the manager says sorry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ruben about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we can't plan anything big for a while, not a flat, not a holiday. Ruben worries that self-driving buses come too. My boyfriend Ruben drives the number 14 bus, and in two years neither of us knows who'll still have a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change how you feel about learning the new tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'm too slow at that and I'd hate it. I'd rather find more places with a real piano.

say: I'd say the **government** must put people before companies, fast.
I'd call **two years** mad to anyone who asked.
think: **Ballet mornings** go first because class music is easy for a computer.
The **hotel lounge** empties if business travellers lose their jobs.
do: Stop **extra spending** and protect four months of savings.
Look for a **second hotel** or restaurant wanting live piano.
feel: **Anxious**, picturing the lounge getting **quieter** until she's let go.
S2.quote: My boyfriend Ruben drives the number 14 bus, and in two years neither of us knows who'll still have a job.
fieldNote: She sees her hotel risk through **guests' jobs**, not robot pianists.
Her boyfriend's **bus job** feels exposed too, which adds to the worry.

steps.text: Cut all extra spending and protect four months of savings

Teach beginner piano to children at home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to plan, so the government should help people like me find other work. I'd say it calmly though, I'm not one for marches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lose the ballet mornings in a couple of years and the hotel would hang on longer. Live piano isn't screen work, so maybe until 2034, if people still travel. Five years is enough to build up pupils.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build up home teaching to eight or ten children over two years. I'd keep the hotel as long as they'd have me. I'd save a bit more from each fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more like a worry I'd carry around than one that keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you think parents would still pay for a person to teach piano?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd want a person for my own child. A child needs someone to tell them their wrist is too high and that they did well. A machine can play Für Elise perfectly, but a seven-year-old practises for a smile, not a score.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does teaching appeal to you, or is it the only option?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both. I never planned to teach. But I like children more than hotel guests, if I'm truthful.

think: The **ballet mornings** go in a couple of years, the hotel lasts longer.
Five years is enough to build up **home pupils**.

steps.text: Build up home piano teaching to eight children within two years
Keep playing the hotel lounge four evenings a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and lots can change. I'd be sensible about it, not alarmist. Most people I know would carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'd be thirty-seven before the thinking machines arrive, and forty before any robot pianist. I'd have time to build a teaching business slowly. The hotel probably still renews me once or twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep both jobs for now and start a few home pupils in the next year. I'd maybe take the piano teaching exams, the graded diplomas, so parents trust me. I'd keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. Uneasy at the back of my mind, but it's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Ruben and you plan anything differently with that long a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably look at buying a small flat in a few years, with room for a piano. I'd want a flat with one wall strong enough for an upright piano, because that wall is my pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger pianist starting out today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn to teach as well as play. Playing the piano gets you hired for a night, but teaching the piano gets you hired for years.

I'd stay **sensible**, not alarmist, like most people I know.
think: I'd be **thirty-seven** before thinking machines and forty before robot pianists.
There's time to build a **teaching business** slowly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because a robot plays piano, but because the people who sit in the Meridian lounge would lose their jobs and stop coming, and the ballet school would buy an app. What would help is a bit of time and some help finding pupils, maybe the council paying for children's music lessons so families can afford a real teacher.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask if anyone actually listens. Most nights nobody does, and I play anyway. I think that's what a lot of people do at work, and it doesn't show up in any of this.

headlineQuote: I'd want a flat with one wall strong enough for an upright piano, because that wall is my pension.
portrait: Sara is a **27-year-old pianist** who plays ballet classes in the mornings and a hotel lounge at night.
She has a **two-year hotel contract**, about four months saved and a boyfriend who drives a bus.
She's **centre-ground**, dislikes technology and refuses to run any accompaniment app.
She expects the **ballet mornings** to go first and the hotel to last until guests stop coming.
Longer timelines turn her slowly towards **teaching children**, which she finds she likes.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because hotel guests and the ballet school would drop live piano.
whatWouldHelp: **Time**, and help finding pupils, such as **council-paid** children's music lessons.
